title: What really drives our revenue
subtitle: Nine months of orders show product mix matters more than volume

headline: Revenue follows price mix, not order volume, and one in five orders comes back

takeaways.title: Price mix leads
takeaways.text: Unit price tracks revenue more closely than units sold, so shifting mix toward premium products moves the top line most.

takeaways.title: A few big orders
takeaways.text: Average order value sits well above the median: a handful of large orders carry a disproportionate share of revenue.

takeaways.title: Returns are material
takeaways.text: Roughly one in five orders is returned, a real drag on realized revenue that deserves its own investigation.

title: Price, not volume, moves revenue
bullets: Unit price has the strongest relationship with revenue of any field.
Units sold matter, but noticeably less than which product is sold.
Discount shows no strong link to volume, so promotions may not pay.

title: Gizmo leads a close product race
bullets: Gizmo is the most-ordered product, but the three are close.
Mix shifts toward Gizmo would lift revenue if its price holds.

title: Order values are right-skewed
bullets: The median order is far below the largest, so outliers drive averages.
Report medians alongside means when tracking order value.

items.statement: Featuring Gizmo more prominently raises revenue per order.
items.test: A/B test merchandising that leads with Gizmo; compare revenue per order.

items.statement: Deeper discounts do not increase units per order.
items.test: Regress units on discount, controlling for product and region.

items.statement: Return rates differ meaningfully by product.
items.test: Chi-square test of returned versus product on the full order history.

title: Recommended next steps
steps: Join cost data to compute margin per product before changing prices.
Break returns down by product and region to find the root cause.
Run the Gizmo merchandising test for four weeks.
Extend the analysis window to capture seasonality.
